newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Howard may be making the same mistake twice.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Howard may be making the same mistake twice.

text.p: With hindsight, Prime Minister John Howard could have saved himself some trouble if he had dumped his then assistant treasurer, Jim Short, last week.
Is Howard now making the same political mistake with just six days later with Industry Minister John Moore?
The Labor Opposition spent all question time on Tuesday quoting incidents where Moore has made a decision that might have affected a shareholding he holds in a venture capital company.

The opposition said the government, with Moore as industry minister, had taken the decision to maintain the computer bounty in the budget, benefitting companies in which he had an indirect interest, through Bligh Ventures Ltd.

Parliamentary Secretary to the Treasurer Brian Gibson meanwhile was falling on his sword in the Senate, explaining he had discovered that in June he had made a decision benefiting Boral, in which he had an interest.

The issue of ministerial investments has now cost the government a junior minister and a parliamentary secretary. A senior minister is under threat and the Treasurer Peter Costello might have been in trouble but for the political incorrectness of involving his wife (who holds banking shares).
And who knows what else the opposition might be able to dig up?
The government needs to deflect the whole issue and Howard has moved to do so by implying that the real problem is the code, not the ministers.
Howard told parliament that he wanted a system introduced to let ministers hold shares through blind trusts, so that they could keep their commercial interests at arms length.

Of course it is not the fault of the code. As far as is practicable, ministers should not be allowed to make decisions that affect their own wealth, and Howard will be doing well if he can distract political attention from that simple notion.
Interestingly, there has always been an exception to that rule: primary industries ministers are very commonly farmers.
